documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                      )
         PJM Interconnection, L.L.C                   )                  Docket No. ER26-1479-000
                                                      )



    LIMITED PROTEST OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED AND THE SOLAR ENERGY
                         INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION


         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission”)

Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Advanced Energy United (“United”)2 and the Solar Energy

Industries Association (“SEIA”)3 submit these comments in response to PJM Interconnection,

L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) February 23, 2026 compliance filing4 to address the Commission’s directives

in its December 18, 2025 Order (“Co-location Order”)5 to revise its behind the meter generation

(“BTMG”) tariffs, establish three new transmission service tariffs, and revise its study

processes.6

         PJM’s compliance with the Co-Location Order will impact the cost and speed at which

the region is able to serve the massive influx of new large loads being built. PJM’s proposed




1
  18 C.F.R. § 385.211 (2025).
2
  Advanced Energy United is a national association of businesses that are making the energy we use secure,
clean and affordable. Advanced Energy United is the only industry association in the United States that represents
the full range of advanced energy technologies and services, both grid-scale and distributed. Advanced energy
includes energy efficiency, demand response, energy storage, wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, electric vehicles, and
more. The comments expressed in this filing represent the position of Advanced Energy United but may not
represent the views of any particular member.
3
  The comments contained in this filing represent the position of SEIA as a trade organization on behalf of the solar
industry, but do not necessarily reflect the views of any particular member with respect to any issue.
4
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 60-Day Compliance Filing for Co-Located Load Related Revisions to Open Access
Transmission Tariff to Comply with Commission Order in Docket No. EL25-49, et al., ER26-1479 (February 23,
2026) (“PJM Compliance Filing”).
5
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217, at PP 2, 161, 231-36 (2025) (“Co-Location Order”).
6
  Co-Location Order at P 160.
 tariff revisions fundamentally fail to comply with the directive and intent of the Co-Location

Order, which was to encourage flexible load that is able to interconnect quickly with limited

impact on the grid. Instead, PJM’s Compliance Filing imposes unnecessary barriers on the

resources most able to be built quickly to serve new and existing load and maintain grid

reliability amidst the current surge in demand. The Commission should reject PJM’s Compliance

Filing and direct it to refile tariffs that comply with the requirements of the Co-Location Order to

accommodate new loads in an affordable, reliable, and efficient manner.

       I.       Background
            PJM is facing an unprecedented surge of new load wanting to connect to the system,

including a massive influx of data centers and large-scale manufacturing. This has placed

significant stress on the region’s ability to meet its resource adequacy requirements, at a time

when the interconnection of new generation has been stalled as PJM works through a backlog of

requests and implements new reforms. Developers and large loads have turned to co-location

strategies and BTMG as solutions to this growing problem.

            The Commission recognized the need to provide greater regulatory certainty to guide

increased interest in both existing and novel behind-the-meter configurations when it issued the

Co-Location Order. Specifically, the Commission found PJM’s tariff to be unjust and

unreasonable because it did not include service options that allow customers to be flexible during

certain conditions.7 The Commission ordered PJM to develop three new transmission services

that would allow loads to take non-firm service for all or part of their facilities on a temporary or

permanent basis.8 As part of that Order, the Commission also directed PJM to revise its BTMG




7
    Id at P 2
8
    Id at P 176-177.


                                                   2
 rules.9 In response to the Co-Location Order, PJM held stakeholder meetings in an effort to

inform members and solicit feedback on the proposals. While PJM made modest revisions in

response to this feedback, the Compliance Filing still falls short of the requirements of the Co-

Location Order.


     II.      Limited Protest

              A. BTMG rules are overly restrictive and do not accommodate optimized
                 hybrid configurations
           PJM’s Compliance Filing fails to comply with the Co-Location Order’s clear directive to

set a net megawatt (“MW”) materiality threshold based on the amount of load a customer may

net using BTMG and should therefore be rejected. The Co-Location Order directed PJM to

“maintain the current BTMG rules for customers that fall below a new MW materiality threshold

for the amount of load at a particular electrical location that Network Customers may net using

BTMG” and for customers utilizing BTMG arrangements that meet certain transition and

grandfathering criteria.10 In response, PJM proposes a 50 MW materiality threshold for BTMG,

measured based on the cumulative nameplate rating of all BTMG at the same electrical location,

excluding backup generation and BTMG that meets certain transition and grandfathering

criteria.11 While the exclusion of backup generation appropriately avoids disincentivizing

reliance on backup generation that can bring a net benefit to the reliability of the system, PJM’s

application of the 50 MW threshold to the nameplate capacity of the BTMG, rather than the

amount of load the customer may net, as required by the Co-Location Order, is a material

deviation from the requirements of the Co-Location Order and should be rejected. PJM’s


9
  Id at P 179.
10
   Id. (emphasis added).
11
   PJM Compliance Filing, Transmittal Letter at page 11-14; Tariff, Part VIII, Subpart A, section 400
Definitions R.


                                                         3
 deviation will unnecessarily constrain the different configurations of BTMG that may otherwise

emerge based on the Co-Location Order’s requirements.

       The Commission’s Order is appropriately focused on the impact of netting on the PJM

system, whereas PJM’s definition is myopically focused on the nameplate capacity of the

BTMG. This proposed threshold is inconsistent with how PJM assesses capacity accreditation in

the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) and lacks the necessary flexibility to accommodate

resource diversity and hybrid configurations such as storage paired with solar or other

technologies that have compatible production profiles and are capable of providing firm capacity

via precise operational control. Modern BTMG assets are equipped with advanced telemetry

systems and the capability to allow for instant load following. These resources can be leaned on

during times of transmission congestion and limited capacity. Consider a 30 MW industrial

customer with existing firm service and sufficient land to host large-scale behind-the-meter

resources. A hybrid configuration consisting of 30 MW of solar PV and 30 MW of battery

storage—designed to operate as non-export and provide microgrid capabilities during grid

outages—would no longer be available under the cumulative 50 MW nameplate limit. This is the

case even though the configuration is intended only to serve the customer’s 30 MW peak load.

Other reasons why a BTMG asset may have a nameplate capacity that exceeds the customer’s

netting include (1) a facility serving an industrial site with thermal as well as electrical needs; (2)

a project that is oversized to account for uptime and availability considerations to meet

performance and redundancy needs; or (3) a project that is oversized at the onset to account for

near- and long-term degradation.

       Because PJM failed to follow the Commission’s directive in this regard, the Commission

should reject PJM’s proposal. Any revised proposal from PJM must set a materiality threshold




                                                  4
 based on the customer’s netting, not the nameplate capacity of the BTMG. A reasonable

approach would be to permit facilities to exceed the proposed 50 MW nameplate capacity

threshold for BTMG provided that the customer’s netting is limited to 50 MW. This allowance

should be contingent upon the facility utilizing approved telemetry and automated system

controls to ensure the customer’s actual impact on the transmission system remains within

specified, safe limits. Manual 14D already includes metering and reporting requirements for

BTMG and loads utilizing BTMG, which should allow PJM to address the majority of concerns

regarding the effect of netting load via BTMG; to the extent PJM believes that updates to these

provisions of the manuals are necessary to implement additional reasonable telemetry and

control requirements necessary to effectuate netting, PJM may work with stakeholders through

normal channels to do so. Measuring a resource by its theoretical maximum output—rather than

its actual, controlled impact—is a regulatory relic that undermines the benefits of the Co-

Location Order. PJM failed to follow the requirements of the Co-Location Order and its

Compliance Filing should therefore be rejected.

             B. Transition and Grandfathering Rules Must Ensure a Smooth Transition to
                Avoid Adverse Reliability Impacts
         Generators and both existing and new large loads have turned to the existing BTMG rules

as a logical response to conditions in the PJM region. The PJM Base Residual Auction (“BRA”)

sends capacity price signals to customers and developers of the supply and demand on the

system. The temporary closure of PJM’s interconnection queue to new generation,12 significant




12
   PJM effectively closed its interconnection process to new applicants in 2022 and expects to initiate the first cluster
study of new requests in April 2026. See “PJM Completes Interconnection Reform Transition Cycle 1 Studies”
(September 22, 2025). https://insidelines.pjm.com/pjm-completes-interconnection-reform-transition-cycle-1-
studies/#:~:text=In%20July%202023%2C%20PJM%20began,and%20coal%20(29%20MW).



                                                           5
 price increases in the BRA,13 anticipated resource adequacy shortfalls in coming years, and

rising transmission costs and significant transmission upgrade needs have resulted in some end

use customers making business decisions to address these issues outside of PJM’s markets.

Those efforts have resulted in investments that will lead to additional generation and

transmission capacity—albeit behind the meter— in the PJM region at a time when such capacity

is sorely needed. Upending those efforts, as PJM’s proposal does, would result in financial injury

to the parties involved as they are prevented from participating as anticipated due to a new

regulatory requirement that was not in place when capital was allocated to the development and

deployment of these projects. Even worse, PJM’s proposal would harm reliability and

affordability in the PJM region by causing existing projects to cease operations and/or by leading

customers to abandon planned projects already well underway. The PJM region needs more

valuable capacity as soon as possible and should not be creating regulatory barriers that counter-

productively disincentivize already planned or capitalized projects from continuing to be

available in PJM.

        The Co-Location Order appropriately recognized the potential disruption of a transition

to new BTMG and co-location requirements, and directed PJM to take two steps to avoid adverse

impacts: (1) grandfathering entities with existing contracts through the end of the term of such

agreements, and (2) implementing a three-year transition period for any existing BTMG not

eligible for grandfathered treatment.14

        In response to the first directive, PJM proposes to “allow existing BTMG arrangements to

qualify for legacy treatment so long as there is an existing contractual agreement for the purpose


13
   The BRA Increased by over 1,000% between the 2024/2025 planning year to the 2027/2028 planning year even
with a price cap instituted. See “2027/2028 Base Residual Auction Report (December 17, 2025.
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/markets-ops/rpm/rpm-auction-info/2027-2028/2027-2028-bra-report.pdf
14
   Co-Location Order at P 179.


                                                      6
 of effectuating a BTMG arrangement (e.g., bilateral agreement, interconnection agreement, etc.)

that was in effect prior to December 18, 2025.”15 In response to the second directive, PJM

proposes that any existing retail BTMG not eligible for grandfathering would continue to be

eligible to participate as BTMG through December 18, 2028.16

        The Commission must balance concerns about expediently addressing unjust and

unreasonable rates with concerns from parties that have relied on the existing Tariff.17 For the

proposed changes to avoid worsening PJM’s tight resource adequacy conditions, the

grandfathering and transition rules must be robust enough to protect BTMG projects that are

already in various stages of development. Planning, constructing, and interconnecting these

resources is a multi-year process including significant capital outlays that rely on longstanding

market fundamentals; any new rules must endeavor to respect the progress made by existing

projects. PJM’s Compliance Filing fails to ensure a smooth and predictable transition and is

contrary to the Co-Location Order’s requirements regarding grandfathering. Therefore, the

Compliance Filing should be rejected.

        First, to prevent any disruptive administrative burdens, any project “in process” as of the

transition date should be eligible for grandfathering if it has made significant progress toward

completion. This should include projects that have contractual arrangements in place, even if

they are not yet fully operational. To reach the stage of development where a contractual

arrangement has been put in place, there have already been significant resources invested in a

project. Preventing a project from executing on that contractual obligation simply because it has

not completed construction as of the date that the Order was issued, which was unknowable



15
   Transmittal Letter at 9.
16
   Transmittal Letter at 11.
17
   See Co-Location Order, P 223.


                                                 7
 when the project was initiated, would cause harm to the market and strand significant

investments that were made to add flexibility to the system. PJM’s Compliance Filing as it stands

will result in significant stranded assets and should therefore be rejected.

           PJM states that it “will explore with stakeholders whether Manual language should be

developed to help elaborate on what types of agreements may qualify.”18 To help inform such

discussion, the Commission should clarify that such agreements may include utility

interconnection study agreements; engineering, procurement, and construction contracts; and any

form of binding agreement between the BTMG developer and the load. In the Co-Location

Order, the Commission “acknowledge[d] the possibility that entities may also have contracted

for the specific purpose of effectuating a BTMG arrangement” and directed PJM to grandfather

such entities “[t]o the extent an entity is a party to an existing contract for such a purpose.”19 The

Commission should clarify that the above listed agreements or any other agreement “for the

specific purpose of effectuating a BTMG arrangement” should qualify as a “contractual

arrangement” eligible for grandfathering under PJM’s proposed Retail BTMG definition.

Without this clarity, developers that have spent significant time and effort responding to the

existing regulatory and market realities face the risk of delay and additional regulatory burdens

that could remove projects already under study or even under construction.

           Second, to further avoid harm to projects already well underway, PJM should shift back

its grandfathering date to the effective date of PJM’s compliance filing. As noted above,

customers and developers have been pursuing BTMG opportunities under PJM’s current rules in

response to market and grid conditions. Prior to the issuance of the Show Cause Order, it was

unknown to both customers and developers whether, when, and how PJM’s current rules to


18
     Transmittal Letter at n32.
19
     Co-Location Order at P 224.


                                                  8
 BTMG would be changed. Even today, there remains significant uncertainty overhanging new

rules for BTMG in the PJM region, with key questions such as the materiality threshold for

Retail BTMG pending before the Commission. PJM acknowledges these lingering uncertainties

when it states that the effective date for its own compliance is uncertain.20 Setting the

grandfathering date at the date of issuance of the Co-location Order would unnecessarily cut off

projects that were moving forward in good faith under then-existing rules. Furthermore, the

BTMG transition must be considered in the context of the new co-location framework. Projects

previously operating or moving forward under the BTMG construct that become ineligible for

Retail BTMG treatment (i.e., because they are ineligible for grandfathering and exceed the

materiality threshold) will be compelled to consider shifting to the new co-location pathways if

they do not wish to cease operations or halt development. Setting the BTMG grandfathering date

earlier than the effective date for the new co-location pathways would leave a problematic gap

for projects already underway that will exacerbate regulatory and market uncertainty to the

detriment of reliability in PJM. The three-year transition is not an antidote to this uncertainty, as

it provides only temporary relief and does not change the ultimate outcome for projects

previously pursuing permanent BTMG status.

           Third, PJM’s proposal is currently unclear whether grandfathering status applies to the

BTMG asset or to the site itself, which makes the proposal unjust and unreasonable.

Grandfathering is not merely a matter of fairness; it is a matter of resource optimization. Existing

industrial sites hold significant potential to provide additional flexibility to the grid if they are

permitted to expand their BTMG footprint. For example, an industrial site that has an existing

contract with a 60 MW co-generation facility may also have the ability to add some amount of



20
     Transmittal Letter at 35.


                                                   9
 behind-the-meter battery storage; if grandfathering applies to the customer site, the 60 MW co-

generation facility would presumably remain under Retail BTMG, but even 10 MW of battery

storage would not be eligible to participate as BTMG. However, if it is the co-generation facility

that is grandfathered, the customer should still be eligible to add BTMG up to the new

materiality threshold, and the additional 10 MW of battery storage could participate as BTMG.

When justifying the 50 MW materiality threshold for Retail BTMG going forward, PJM explains

that “a lower threshold of 10 or 20 MW would likely exclude from Retail BTMG a much larger

volume of retail customers whose grid impacts are small or de minimis when compared with the

Co-Located Load coming online today.”21 PJM also rightly identifies that existing BTMG

arrangements have been in place for decades in some cases, with no known operational issues.22

Grandfathering the generation while allowing these existing customers to pursue additional

BTMG below the materiality threshold is a logical extension of PJM’s observation that the

existing BTMG at these sites is not problematic, and additions below the materiality threshold

would have little or no impact. If the Commission accepts PJM’s proposal in this regard, the

Commission must clarify that customers with existing BTMG generation that is grandfathered

can add additional new BTMG.

           Clarifying that customers with grandfathered BTMG are allowed a “clean slate” to pursue

additional BTMG up to the materiality threshold would also allow the existing customer base in

the PJM region to be part of the solution to PJM’s urgent resource adequacy and grid

infrastructure needs. Many of these existing customers have neither the desire nor the economic

incentive to pursue the newer, more complex “co-location” pathways proposed by PJM, and

smaller projects (like the 10 MW battery in the example above) will almost certainly be boxed


21
     Transmittal Letter at 12.
22
     Id.


                                                 10
 out by the cost and complexity of undergoing the full PJM interconnection process. PJM

expresses concern in its Compliance Filing that existing Retail BTMG resources may forgo

interconnecting into the PJM system if excluded from Retail BTMG, and that this would

exacerbate reliability concerns.23 By the same logic, allowing customers with grandfathered

BTMG to pursue new BTMG that they would not otherwise pursue under a co-location

arrangement would have the effect of improving reliability by reducing the capacity needs of

these customers.

           To maximize grid reliability and customer benefit, the Commission should clarify that

PJM’s Compliance Filing allows loads with grandfathered BTMG a “clean slate” to net an

additional 50 MW of BTMG. If PJM’s Compliance Filing is interpreted to disallow the

expansion of BTMG on these established sites, it will effectively prevent existing industrial loads

from contributing new flexibility to the system, which is an unjust and unreasonable result. The

PJM system will be more resilient if it does not rely solely on new loads to deliver additional

grid flexibility. Forcing established industrial players to pursue co-location arrangements in order

to add any incremental behind-the-meter generation, even when that new generation is below the

agreed materiality threshold, ignores "low-hanging fruit" that could benefit the reliability of the

PJM region. The Commission should clarify this is not the case.

               C. Streamlining Interconnection for Non-Exporting Co-Located Facilities

           PJM’s proposal to require site-located generation to enter the interconnection queue24 is

unjust and unreasonable. The PJM Compliance Filing requires both new and existing BTMG

arrangements that exceed the materiality threshold and do not qualify for grandfathering



23
     Transmittal Letter at 13.
24
     PJM Compliance Filing at page 24.


                                                   11
 provisions to transition toward a co-location arrangement, which entails pursuing a full

interconnection agreement with PJM. While it is recognized that co-located loads and generation

have a distinct cost and impact on the grid, this does not justify imposing the full, standard

interconnection process on resources that do not intend to export power to the grid. Shifting non-

exporting generating resources to a co-location framework should not, by default, trigger new

interconnection requirements. This requirement would artificially inflate the number of projects

in an already backlogged queue and force projects that will never export power to undergo

studies intended for exporting generators. These projects do not require deliverability given their

intent to serve only the co-located load; given that they will rarely, if ever, trigger network

upgrades, subjecting them to the standard queue process is a purely administrative hurdle with no

technical or reliability benefit, but significant burden for such projects. The PJM Compliance

Filing is therefore unjust and unreasonable and should be rejected.

       To avoid further slowing the interconnection queue while still ensuring adequate

screening of non-exporting co-located generation, PJM should be encouraged to instead establish

a streamlined, expedited process specifically for resources that do not intend to export to the

grid. A streamlined process should be specifically established for resources that operate as non-

exporting co-located generating facilities. Shifting these resources to the new co-location

framework is a recognition of the grid impact caused by the co-located load, but this transition

should not necessitate a full-scale interconnection study for the generation component. In lieu of

the traditional interconnection process, PJM should implement an expedited review track that

focuses on requirements that are proportional to the actual technical impact the resources have on

the grid. This would allow PJM to maintain visibility and safety without subjecting non-




                                                 12
 exporting co-located resources to the multi-year delays and costs associated with the traditional

generator interconnection queue.

   III.      Conclusion

          Quickly clarifying new rules for BTMG and co-location pathways in PJM will bring

desperately needed regulatory and market certainty that will unlock grid flexibility and increase

speed to power while protecting reliability and affordability. Yet overly rigid rules that hinder

innovative behind the meter configurations; transition and grandfathering rules that limit, rather

than expand, opportunities for behind the meter and co-located resources to contribute to meeting

resource adequacy needs in PJM; and unnecessarily cumbersome interconnection pathways that

dampen participation will erode the utility of this regulatory certainty. Swift Commission action

rejecting PJM’s Compliance Filing and directing revisions to rectify these shortcomings and

comply with the Co-Location Order will deliver greater impact and a more durable set of market

participation pathways for co-located and behind-the-meter resources in PJM.

          Respectfully submitted,
